title: Say It Again
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: This brief but cogent leadership piece argues that the fundamental mistake leaders make after communicating a strategy or vision is to move on after saying it once. The culprit is the 'curse of knowledge' -- the cognitive bias where familiarity with a subject makes it hard to reconstruct what it was like not to know it. A leader who has spent weeks developing a strategy experiences it as obvious; their team encounters it as new, and some of them were distracted, confused, or simply forgot it by the next day. The 'rule of seven' from 1930s marketing research -- that an audience needs roughly seven exposures before acting -- applies with equal force inside organizations. The article's practical guidance: vary the delivery while keeping the core message identical, and measure completion not by when you said the message but by when your team can articulate, apply, and recognize deviations from it without you in the room.
points: The 'curse of knowledge' means that leaders who have internalized their strategy find it nearly impossible to remember what encountering it for the first time felt like -- causing them to systematically underestimate how many repetitions their team needs.

The rule of seven, developed in 1930s marketing, holds that audiences need roughly seven exposures before acting; research inside organizations pushes this number higher, meaning a single all-hands communication is almost certainly insufficient.

Repetition signals importance in ways that one-time delivery cannot: when leaders return to the same message across different contexts and formats, the organization learns that this direction is real and durable, not a monthly theme.

The practical method: hold the core message constant while varying delivery -- reference the strategy in a one-on-one, connect it to a customer story in an all-hands, embed it in a question at the leadership offsite -- so it appears in the team's context, not just the leader's.

A message is done not when the leader has said it but when team members can articulate it, apply it to problems the leader was not present for, and recognize when a decision moves away from it -- a much higher bar than most leaders set.
quotes: The more you know, the harder it becomes to imagine what your audience is encountering for the first time. A few understood it perfectly and will forget it by the next day.
What is clear across the research is that a single delivery rarely moves people to action. Repetition also does something that one-time communication cannot: it signals that you mean it.
Vary the Delivery, Not the Message The risk of strategic repetition is that it becomes mechanical. What works is holding the core message steady while varying how you carry it.

Ask a question in a leadership offsite that can only be answered well if people have internalized the direction. It is done when your team can articulate it, apply it to a problem you were not in the room for, and recognize when a decision moves away from it.
